1.title: Highly Available and Fault-Tolerant Architectures
1.text: Welcome to Module five: Highly Available and Fault-Tolerant Architectures. This module covers task statement two point two, the second task of Domain two. You will learn how to survive a failed server, a failed zone and a failed Region: redundancy, failover, routing, disaster recovery, automation and visibility. The exam gives you a failure and a target, and asks you to choose the design.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Design for high availability and fault tolerance across Availability Zones and Regions. Remove single points of failure, and choose failover and routing approaches. Select a disaster recovery strategy from the R P O and the R T O. Use automation and immutable infrastructure, and manage quotas and throttling. And pick services for visibility, and for legacy and non-cloud workloads.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lantern and Loom Survives a Bad Day
1.text: Lantern and Loom had a bad day. A power event in one zone took the whole shop offline for forty minutes. Leaders now ask: what if a whole Region fails? Their targets are to lose at most minutes of data, and to recover in about an hour. And an old inventory server cannot be changed. Your job is to choose the redundancy, the failover and the recovery design.

1.title: High Availability, Fault Tolerance and Resilience
1.text: Three terms to separate. High availability means the workload keeps serving with minimal interruption when a component fails, using redundancy and fast failover. Fault tolerance means the workload keeps running without interruption through a failure, at higher cost and complexity. Resilience is the ability to recover from disruption and keep meeting demand. Availability is a percent of time: ninety-nine point nine percent allows about eight point eight hours of downtime a year; ninety-nine point nine nine percent about fifty-three minutes; and ninety-nine point nine nine nine percent about five minutes. Set the target from business requirements. Exam tip: each extra nine costs more, so choose the availability the business actually needs.

1.title: Removing Single Points of Failure
1.text: Start by removing single points of failure. Use a load balancer and an Auto Scaling group that span two or more Availability Zones. Put one N A T gateway in each zone, point each zone's route table at its own gateway, and use a Multi-A Z database. S three, DynamoDB and S Q S already run across zones. Then hunt for the singles: one instance, one zone, one D N S record, one manual step. The figure shows two zones, each with application servers and a N A T gateway, a spanning load balancer, and a database with a standby. Exam tip: if one thing failing takes the workload down, it is a single point of failure.

1.title: Multi-AZ or Multi-Region?
1.text: Multi-A Z or Multi-Region? Multi-A Z protects against a data center or zone failure. Zones are far enough apart to avoid shared failures, and close enough for synchronous replication. It is the default for high availability, at moderate cost and effort. Multi-Region protects against a whole Region failing. The Regions are far apart, so replication is asynchronous. It also helps with compliance distance and lower latency for global users, but costs more and takes more effort. Exam tip: a zone-level failure needs Multi-A Z; a Region-level disaster, or a distance rule, needs Multi-Region.

1.title: Failover Patterns and Health Checks
1.text: Failover comes in two shapes. Active-passive means a standby takes traffic only after a failure. Active-active means every site serves traffic. Health checks detect failures, and load balancers, Auto Scaling and Route fifty-three act on them. Automatic failover can trigger on false alarms, so many teams use a manual start with automated steps. During failover, rely on the data plane, not on control plane changes. Distributed design patterns help too: timeouts, retries with backoff, queues, stateless services and idempotent work. Exam tip: pre-provision what recovery needs, so failover does not depend on creating resources during the outage.

1.title: Amazon Route 53 Routing Policies
1.text: Route fifty-three has eight routing policies. Simple serves one resource for a domain. Failover sets up active-passive failover. Latency sends users to the Region with the best latency. Weighted splits traffic in set proportions. Geolocation routes by the user's location. Geoproximity routes by resource location, with an optional shift. I P based routes by the user's I P address range. And multivalue answer returns up to eight healthy records at random. Exam tip: backup site is failover; fastest Region is latency; gradual rollout is weighted.

1.title: Route 53 Health Checks and DNS Failover
1.text: Here is how D N S failover works. Failover records have a primary and a secondary, with a health check on the primary. When the check fails, Route fifty-three answers with the secondary. Alias records can evaluate target health for A W S resources. Remember that D N S caching and the T T L delay a switch. Global Accelerator uses static I P addresses and avoids D N S caching. The figure shows users reaching Route fifty-three, which answers with the primary Region until its health check fails. Exam tip: automatic D N S failover to a standby Region means Route fifty-three failover routing with health checks.

1.title: Database High Availability
1.text: For the database tier, there are several options. An R D S Multi-A Z D B instance keeps one synchronous standby in another zone and fails over automatically; the standby does not serve reads. An R D S Multi-A Z D B cluster has two readable standbys. Aurora copies its storage across three zones, and replicas can take over. Aurora Global Database replicates across Regions, with typical lag under a second, and you can promote a secondary in under a minute. DynamoDB global tables give multi-Region reads and writes, where the last writer wins. Exam tip: to survive a zone failure, use Multi-A Z; to survive a Region failure, use Aurora Global Database or global tables.

1.title: Amazon RDS Proxy
1.text: Amazon R D S Proxy is a managed proxy that pools and shares database connections. It makes applications more resilient to database failures, because it connects to a standby while preserving application connections. It absorbs surges, and queues or throttles connections the database cannot serve yet. It supports I A M authentication and Secrets Manager credentials, and works for most applications with no code changes. It is a strong fit for Lambda, which opens many short connections. Exam tip: connection storms or slow failover reconnects point to R D S Proxy.

1.title: Storage Durability and Availability
1.text: Separate durability from availability. Durability means data is not lost; availability means you can reach it. S three stores data across multiple Availability Zones and is designed for eleven nines of durability. An E B S volume is replicated inside one zone, so use snapshots to protect it across zones and Regions. E F S is Regional, stored across zones. Replicate to another Region with S three replication, snapshot copies and A W S Backup. And turn on S three Versioning to undo mistaken deletes. Exam tip: block storage lives in one zone, so protect it with snapshots; object storage spans zones by default.

2.title: RPO and RTO
2.text: Two numbers drive disaster recovery. The R P O, or recovery point objective, is how much data loss, measured in time, is acceptable. The R T O, or recovery time objective, is how long the service may be down. Backup or replication frequency sets the R P O, and the recovery process sets the R T O. Both come from business requirements, and tighter targets cost more. The figure shows a disaster marker, with the R P O bracket before it and the R T O bracket after it. Exam tip: R P O looks back at lost data; R T O looks forward at downtime.

2.title: Four Disaster Recovery Strategies
2.text: There are four disaster recovery strategies. Backup and restore copies data to the recovery Region, and you redeploy everything after a disaster. Pilot light replicates data continuously and keeps core infrastructure ready, but the application servers are switched off. Warm standby keeps a scaled-down but running copy that can take traffic at once. And multi-site active-active runs full capacity in several Regions, all serving users. The figure shows the four steps rising, with cost and recovery speed rising too. Exam tip: the more you keep running in the recovery Region, the faster and costlier the recovery.

2.title: Comparing the Strategies
2.text: Here is the comparison. Backup and restore runs only backups in the recovery Region; recovery takes hours, and the cost is lowest. Pilot light runs the data stores only; recovery takes tens of minutes, at low cost. Warm standby runs a scaled-down full stack; recovery takes minutes, at medium cost. Active-active runs a full-size stack; recovery is near zero, at the highest cost. Pilot light cannot take requests until you turn on servers, while warm standby can, at reduced capacity. Exam tip: read the R T O and R P O, then pick the cheapest strategy that still meets both.

2.title: Building the Recovery Region
2.text: How do you build the recovery Region? Replicate the data with S three replication, R D S read replicas, Aurora Global Database, or DynamoDB global tables. Switch traffic with Route fifty-three health checks, Global Accelerator, or CloudFront origin failover. Promote the replica, and scale out the application with Auto Scaling. Redeploy infrastructure with infrastructure as code. Keep service quotas high enough in the recovery Region. Test failover regularly. A W S Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates servers using the pilot light approach. Exam tip: a recovery plan you have not tested is a guess.

2.title: Service Quotas and Throttling
2.text: Service Quotas shows your quotas from one place and lets you request increases. Quotas are set per account and per Region; some are adjustable and some are fixed. A standby Region needs the same quotas as production, or scale-out at failover will fail. Monitor utilization, and set alarms before you reach a limit. Throttling returns errors when you exceed a rate, so use retries with exponential backoff and jitter. Services such as A P I Gateway and Lambda also throttle requests. Exam tip: raise quotas in the recovery Region before the disaster, not during it.

2.title: Automation and Immutable Infrastructure
2.text: Automation keeps infrastructure consistent. With infrastructure as code, CloudFormation describes resources in a template and builds the same stack repeatedly, in many Regions. With immutable infrastructure, you replace servers from a new golden A M I instead of patching them. Auto Scaling replaces unhealthy instances automatically. Systems Manager automates patching and operations, and Service Catalog offers approved products. Keep templates in version control, so changes are trackable and reversible. Clicks in the Management Console do not repeat, but templates and scripts do. Exam tip: repeatable, identical environments in another Region means CloudFormation; replace, do not patch.

2.title: Systems Manager, Service Catalog, Proton and the Well-Architected Tool
2.text: Four governance services appear on the exam. A W S Systems Manager manages nodes at scale: patching, Session Manager, Run Command, Automation and Parameter Store, with no bastion hosts. A W S Service Catalog is a catalog of approved products, with constraints, for self-service launch. A W S Proton offers templates for standard application stacks and C I C D. The Well-Architected Tool reviews a workload against the framework's pillars and gives an improvement plan. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, the documentation announces Proton end of support on the seventh of October, twenty twenty-six, so check its status. Exam tip: operate fleets with Systems Manager; approved self-service products come from Service Catalog.

2.title: Workload Visibility: X-Ray, Health and Grafana
2.text: Several services give you visibility. A W S X-Ray shows traces of requests through your services, and a service map to find bottlenecks and errors. The A W S Health Dashboard shows A W S service events and events that affect your resources, and events also reach EventBridge. Amazon Managed Grafana builds dashboards over CloudWatch, X-Ray and other data sources. Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus provides Prometheus-compatible metrics, especially for containers. CloudWatch metrics, logs and alarms come in module seven. Exam tip: which downstream call is slow or failing is X-Ray; is A W S having a problem is the Health Dashboard.

2.title: Improving Reliability of Legacy Applications
2.text: What if the application cannot change? A W S Application Migration Service, which the documentation now calls A W S Transform M G N, rehosts servers with continuous block-level replication and short cutovers, with no application changes. A W S Application Discovery Service collects server usage and dependencies for planning. R D S Proxy, load balancers and Route fifty-three add resilience without code changes, Elastic Disaster Recovery protects servers without changing them, and VMware Cloud on A W S runs existing VMware workloads unchanged. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, Application Discovery Service is closed to new customers, so check the page. Exam tip: when the application cannot change, add resilience around it: rehost, proxy, balance and replicate.

2.title: Purpose-Built AWS AI Services
2.text: The guide also expects you to know when a ready-made A I, short for artificial intelligence, service is the right managed choice. Amazon Comprehend finds sentiment, entities and key phrases in text. Amazon Polly turns text into lifelike speech. Amazon Transcribe turns speech into text. Amazon Translate translates languages. Amazon Rekognition finds objects, faces and unsafe content in images and video. Amazon Textract extracts text, forms and tables from scanned documents. Amazon Lex builds chatbots. And Amazon SageMaker A I builds, trains and deploys your own models. Exam tip: a ready-made A P I beats running your own models, because there is less to operate and it is built to scale.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: High Availability and Recovery
2.text: Here is what the exam asks. Which redundancy: Multi-A Z, Multi-Region, Auto Scaling, or a Multi-A Z database. Which routing or failover: a Route fifty-three policy, a health check, or Global Accelerator. Which disaster recovery strategy: chosen from the R P O, the R T O and cost. Which automation: CloudFormation, Systems Manager or Service Catalog. And which visibility or legacy tool: X-Ray, Health, R D S Proxy or Application Migration Service. Exam tip: match the failure size to the fix: instance, zone, Region or data corruption.

2.title: Design Check: Lantern and Loom Survives a Bad Day
2.text: Here is the Design Check. Cover the right column and answer each row yourself. Survive the loss of a zone: Auto Scaling across two zones, a load balancer, and Multi-A Z R D S. Database failover without code changes: R D S Multi-A Z, with R D S Proxy for connections. A Region disaster, an hour to recover, minutes of data loss: pilot light, with replicated data and switched-off servers. Switch users to the other Region automatically: Route fifty-three failover with health checks. Rebuild the stack identically elsewhere: CloudFormation templates. Make sure scale-out works at failover: raise Service Quotas in the recovery Region. Find the slow downstream call: X-Ray. And the old inventory server that cannot change: Application Migration Service.

3.title: Module Recap
3.text: Here is the recap. For availability, remove single points of failure; use Multi-A Z for zones and Multi-Region for Regions. For failover, use health checks, Route fifty-three policies, R D S Multi-A Z and R D S Proxy. For disaster recovery, the R P O and R T O choose between backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and active-active. For operations, use infrastructure as code, immutable servers, quotas and retries. And for visibility and legacy, use X-Ray, Health, Application Migration Service and the managed A I services.

3.title: Practice Question 1
3.text: Question one. What does a recovery point objective of fifteen minutes mean for Lantern and Loom's order data? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: no more than fifteen minutes of order data may be lost. R P O is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. The time to restore service is the recovery time objective.

3.title: Practice Question 2
3.text: Question two. Select two. Lantern and Loom runs one E C two instance and one single-A Z R D S database in the same Availability Zone. Which two changes let the shop survive the loss of that zone? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. Run the web tier in an Auto Scaling group across two zones behind a load balancer, and convert the database to a Multi-A Z deployment. A larger instance, nightly snapshots and an Elastic I P address stay in the failed zone or recover slowly.

3.title: Practice Question 3
3.text: Question three. Lantern and Loom wants product pages read aloud for visually impaired shoppers, and wants the sentiment of reviews flagged, with the least operational effort. Which services fit? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Amazon Polly for speech and Amazon Comprehend for sentiment. Both are ready-made services with nothing to train or run. Rekognition and Textract read images and documents, and Lex and Transcribe handle chatbots and speech to text.

3.title: Practice Question 4
3.text: Question four. If a whole Region fails, Lantern and Loom accepts about an hour to recover and a few minutes of data loss, and wants the lowest running cost that still meets this. Which strategy fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: pilot light, with replicated data and switched-off application servers. Continuous replication meets the few-minutes R P O, and turning on servers fits an hour at low cost. Nightly backups miss the R P O, and the other two cost more than needed.

3.title: Practice Question 5
3.text: Question five. The order database must survive the loss of its Availability Zone, with automatic failover and no application changes. Reads can stay on the primary. Which R D S configuration fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: a Multi-A Z D B instance deployment. It keeps a synchronous standby in another zone and fails over automatically through the same endpoint. A replica in the same zone does not help, and a cross-Region replica or backups need manual recovery.

3.title: Practice Question 6
3.text: Question six. Many Lambda functions open database connections that exhaust an R D S database, and failovers disrupt the functions. What should the architect add? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Amazon R D S Proxy in front of the database. It pools and shares connections, and reconnects to the standby during a failover while preserving application connections.

3.title: Practice Question 7
3.text: Question seven. Select two. Which two statements about Amazon Route fifty-three routing policies are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. Failover routing sets up active-passive failover, and latency routing picks the Region with the best latency. Geolocation routes by user location, weighted routing splits traffic in proportions, and simple routing serves a single resource.

3.title: Practice Question 8
3.text: Question eight. After a disaster, Lantern and Loom must recreate its whole environment, including network, load balancers and servers, in a second Region quickly and identically. What is the best approach? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: define it in CloudFormation templates and deploy them to the second Region. Infrastructure as code is repeatable. Runbooks, screenshots and a lone image leave manual steps.

3.title: Practice Question 9
3.text: Question nine. An aging inventory application runs on a physical server in the warehouse and cannot be changed. Lantern and Loom wants to move it to A W S with minimal downtime. Which service fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: A W S Application Migration Service, which the documentation now calls A W S Transform M G N. It rehosts servers with continuous replication and a short cutover, with no application changes.

3.title: Practice Question 10
3.text: Question ten. Requests to Lantern and Loom's A P I pass through A P I Gateway, Lambda and DynamoDB, and some are slow. Which service shows a service map and request traces to find the slow component? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: A W S X-Ray. It collects traces of requests across services and draws a service map that points to bottlenecks and errors.

3.title: Answers at a Glance
3.text: Here are all ten answers. Question one: B. Question two: A and C. Question three: C. Question four: A. Question five: D. Question six: D. Question seven: A and C. Question eight: C. Question nine: A. Question ten: B. In Module six, we start Domain three: high-performing storage.
